# Hot Methods

In a typical program, some methods appear in sampled execution stacks much more
often than others. These frequently observed methods are commonly called
*hot methods*. A hot method is not automatically a bug: it may simply be where
the application does most of its useful work. It is worth investigating when a
method dominates the profile and the work it performs looks more expensive than
the problem requires.

This example creates that situation with a deliberately poor collection choice.
The program stores unique values in a `LinkedList`, then repeatedly checks
whether values from one collection are present in another. JFR and JDK Mission
Control make the expensive method visible, and a small refactoring shows how
choosing a better collection type changes the profile.

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- [JDK Mission Control (JMC)](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/products-jmc9-downloads.html)

## JDK Mission Control (JMC)

1. Download the latest version of JMC from
   [here](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/products-jmc9-downloads.html)

2. Specify the version of Java

   When having multiple versions of Java installed, you may need to specify
   which one to be used by JMC. This can be done through the `jmc.ini` file,
   found under the `Eclipse` directory of where JMC is installed.

   Add the `-vm` option followed by the path to the `bin` directory, as shown
   next.

   ```
   ...
   -vm
   /Users/aattard/.sdkman/candidates/java/current/bin
   ...
   ```

   Please note that this file will contain other information, which is excluded
   for brevity.

## Build the application

The following examples require the application to be built.

```shell
./mvnw clean package
```

(*Optional*) Verify that the JAR file was created

```shell
tree --sort=name './target/libs'
```

There should be one JAR file

```
./target/libs
└── hot-methods-1.0.0.jar

1 directory, 1 file
```

Some of the following commands dump JFR files into a `jfr` directory. Make sure
that the `jfr` directory exists.

```shell
rm -rf './jfr'
mkdir -p './jfr'
```

## Discover hot methods

1. Run the application and trigger the flight recording using the *profile*
   settings.

   ```shell
   java \
     -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=30s,delay=5s,name='HotMethods',filename='./jfr/demo-before-fix.jfr',settings=profile \
     -jar './target/libs/hot-methods-1.0.0.jar'
   ```

   The application will terminate automatically after 40 seconds.

   (*Optional*) Verify that the JFR file was created.

   ```shell
   tree --sort=name './jfr'
   ```

   The recording

   ```
   ./jfr
   └── demo-before-fix.jfr

   1 directory, 1 file
   ```

2. Open the recording file (`./jfr/demo-before-fix.jfr`), in JDK Mission Control

   ```shell
   jmc -open "$(pwd)/jfr/demo-before-fix.jfr"
   ```

   Navigate to *Method Profiling*

   ![Hot Methods](./assets/images/JMC%20-%20Hot%20Methods.png)

   Notice that the top methods appear in sampled stacks far more often than
   the others. That does not prove they are wrong, but it does show where the
   application spends most of its observed execution time.

## Refactor the program

The `HolderOfUniqueValues` class stores unique values in a `LinkedList`. That
choice makes membership checks expensive because `contains()` has to scan the
list. The workload performs many membership checks, so this linear search
becomes visible as a hot path.

A `HashSet` better matches the intent of the class: it stores unique values and
provides efficient membership checks.

1. Update the code

   Copy the updated version of the code from the `fixtures/01-hash-set/`
   directory to replace the `LinkedList` with a `HashSet`.

   ```shell
   rsync --archive 'fixtures/01-hash-set/' .
   ```

   The
   [`HolderOfUniqueValues` class](./src/main/java/demo/HolderOfUniqueValues.java)
   should look like the following example.

   ```java
   package demo;

   import java.util.Collection;
   import java.util.HashSet;

   public final class HolderOfUniqueValues {

       private final Collection<Integer> collection;

       public HolderOfUniqueValues() {
           collection = new HashSet<>();
       }

       public void initialize(final int moduloDivisor) { /* Closed for brevity */ }

       public int countIntersection(final HolderOfUniqueValues other) { /* Closed for brevity */ }
   }
   ```

2. Rebuild the project

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

3. Rerun the application and trigger the flight recording using the *profile*
   settings.

   ```shell
   java \
     -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=30s,delay=5s,name='HotMethods',filename='./jfr/demo-after-fix.jfr',settings=profile \
     -jar './target/libs/hot-methods-1.0.0.jar'
   ```

4. Analyse the recording using JMC (`./jfr/demo-after-fix.jfr`)

   ```shell
   jmc -open "$(pwd)/jfr/demo-after-fix.jfr"
   ```

   Navigate to *Method Profiling*

   ![Better distribution](./assets/images/JMC%20-%20Better%20Distribution.png)

   The sampled execution profile is now less dominated by
   `countIntersection()` than it was before the change.

5. Analyse the recording file (`./jfr/demo-before-fix.jfr`) with a custom
   program

   A Java program can open a JFR recording file, analyse each event, and
   identify the hot methods. The example below reads the recording file, filters
   for `jdk.ExecutionSample` events, and counts how often each method appears
   during sampling. Hot methods are those observed more frequently than others.

   ```java
   #!/usr/bin/env -S java --source 25

   import jdk.jfr.consumer.*;

   import java.io.IOException;
   import java.io.UncheckedIOException;
   import java.nio.file.Path;
   import java.util.HashMap;
   import java.util.List;
   import java.util.Map;
   import java.util.function.Predicate;
   import java.util.regex.Pattern;

   public static void main(final String[] args) {
       if (args.length < 1 || args.length > 2) {
           System.err.println("Usage: ./PrintHotMethods <RECORDING-FILE> [<METHOD-REGEX>]");
           System.exit(1);
       }

       final Path path = Path.of(args[0]);
       final Predicate<String> predicate = createPredicateFromArgs(args);
       final Map<String, Long> results = compute(path, predicate);

       results.entrySet().stream()
               .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed())
               .limit(20)
               .forEach(entry ->
                       System.out.printf("%5d - %s%n", entry.getValue(), entry.getKey())
               );
   }

   private static Map<String, Long> compute(final Path path, final Predicate<String> predicate) {
       final Map<String, Long> results = new HashMap<>();

       try (RecordingFile recordingFile = new RecordingFile(path)) {
           while (recordingFile.hasMoreEvents()) {
               final RecordedEvent event = recordingFile.readEvent();

               if ("jdk.ExecutionSample".equals(event.getEventType().getName())) {
                   final RecordedStackTrace stackTrace = event.getStackTrace();
                   if (stackTrace == null) {
                       continue;
                   }

                   final List<RecordedFrame> frames = stackTrace.getFrames();
                   for (final RecordedFrame frame : frames) {
                       final String method = formatFrame(frame);
                       if (predicate.test(method)) {
                           results.merge(method, 1L, Long::sum);
                       }
                   }
               }
           }
       } catch (final IOException e) {
           throw new UncheckedIOException("Failed to read recording file " + path, e);
       }

       return results;
   }

   private static String formatFrame(final RecordedFrame frame) {
       final RecordedMethod method = frame.getMethod();
       return method.getType().getName() + "." + method.getName() + ":" + frame.getLineNumber();
   }

   private static Predicate<String> createPredicateFromArgs(final String[] args) {
       return args.length == 2
               ? Pattern.compile(args[1]).asMatchPredicate()
               : t -> true;
   }
   ```

   As we are only interested in our own code, the output will include only
   methods belonging to our classes.

   ```shell
   ./src/main/java/PrintHotMethods './jfr/demo-before-fix.jfr' 'demo\..*'
   ```

   The program will print the hot methods from classes within the `demo` package

   ```
    2966 - demo.Main$$Lambda.0x0000000016044a10.run:-1
    2960 - demo.Main.lambda$main$0:26
    2480 - demo.HolderOfUniqueValues.countIntersection:27
     480 - demo.HolderOfUniqueValues.countIntersection:26
       5 - demo.HolderOfUniqueValues.initialize:19
       4 - demo.Main.lambda$main$0:23
       2 - demo.Main.lambda$main$0:22
   ```

   Note the significant difference in sample counts between the top entries and
   the rest. The `countIntersection()` method dominates the application samples
   before the refactoring.

   Let us now compare the sample counts from the second recording, taken after
   the fix was applied.

   ```shell
   ./src/main/java/PrintHotMethods './jfr/demo-after-fix.jfr' 'demo\..*'
   ```

   The program will print the hot methods from classes within the `demo` package

   ```
    2906 - demo.Main$$Lambda.0x000000003a044a10.run:-1
    2322 - demo.HolderOfUniqueValues.initialize:18
    1237 - demo.Main.lambda$main$0:23
    1089 - demo.Main.lambda$main$0:22
     572 - demo.Main.lambda$main$0:26
     304 - demo.HolderOfUniqueValues.countIntersection:29
     268 - demo.HolderOfUniqueValues.countIntersection:25
       3 - demo.Main.lambda$main$0:32
       2 - demo.Main.lambda$main$0:19
       2 - demo.HolderOfUniqueValues.initialize:15
       2 - demo.Main.lambda$main$0:33
       1 - demo.Main.lambda$main$0:30
   ```

   Note that the hot method `countIntersection()` is no longer prominent,
   indicating that the issue has been addressed.
